title: Fat-Soluble Vitamins: Absorption, Vitamin D Status and Vitamin K
summary: Learn why vitamins A, D, E and K depend on fat absorption, why 25(OH)D rather than 1,25(OH)₂D measures vitamin D status, which cut-offs are guideline-dependent, and how vitamin K, warfarin and newborn prophylaxis connect to the vitamin K-dependent proteins.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 27 Hits 6 (vitamin D status = 25(OH)D; two hydroxylations), 7 (fat-soluble vitamins need fat absorption) and 13 (vitamin K antagonism, vitamin K-dependent proteins, newborn vitamin K) and Exam Traps 3 (ordering 1,25(OH)₂D) and 5 (deficiency despite supplements). Checked against Andrès 2024, Dirks 2018, Pilz 2019, Amrein 2020, Saponaro 2020, Araki 2020, van Gorp 2015 and Matthaiou 2023 (all full text via Europe PMC). Nuances: the reviewer’s “target ~30 ng/mL” is one guideline position (the IOM does not conclude there is added benefit of 75 over 50 nmol/L, while the Endocrine Society 2011 guideline treats to at least 75 nmol/L; register flag rv-vitd-target-guideline); the reviewer’s toxicity line “>500 nmol/L” is higher than the sources, which put intoxication hypercalcaemia usually above 375 nmol/L and the IOM’s potential-harm line at a sustained >125 nmol/L (rv-vitd-toxicity-threshold); the source read says 1,25(OH)₂D is almost always normal in deficiency, not “even high”. Not taught (pending): water-soluble deficiency “within weeks”, B12 stores 3–6 years, “PT rises only when undercarboxylated prothrombin falls >50%”.

objectives: Explain why fat malabsorption causes deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K despite adequate intake.
Choose 25(OH)D over 1,25(OH)₂D to assess vitamin D status and state common, guideline-dependent cut-offs.
Name the vitamin K-dependent proteins and explain how warfarin and the newborn state cause vitamin K deficiency effects.

scenes.title: Pills in, vitamins missing
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: an adult with chronic pancreatitis and fatty stools takes a daily multivitamin. Three lab cards: (1) 1,25(OH)₂D within the reference interval; (2) 25(OH)D 9 ng/mL; (3) prolonged PT. Question token: “Normal active vitamin D, daily pills — so why deficient?”

cues.text: Invented case: an adult with chronic pancreatitis and fatty stools takes a multivitamin every day.
The doctor ordered the active vitamin D hormone, and it came back normal. But a second vitamin D test is very low, and the prothrombin time is prolonged.
Which vitamin D result is the right one, and how can daily pills still leave someone deficient?

props.label: Normal active vitamin D, daily pills — so why deficient?

scenes.title: How A, D, E and K get in and get used
scenes.altText: Schematic. Card 1: vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed in the small intestine together with dietary fat; this needs working enterocytes, bile (hepatobiliary function) and pancreatic enzymes. Card 2: vitamin D pathway — skin (UVB) or diet → liver 25-hydroxylation (mainly CYP2R1) → 25(OH)D → kidney 1α-hydroxylation (CYP27B1) → 1,25(OH)₂D, the active hormone; PTH stimulates the renal step, while FGF23 and 1,25(OH)₂D inhibit it. Card 3: vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S; the vitamin K epoxide formed is recycled by vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR).

cues.text: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat, so they are absorbed with dietary fat. That needs a healthy intestinal lining, bile from the liver, and pancreatic enzymes.
Vitamin D from skin or diet is hydroxylated twice: first in the liver, at carbon 25, making 25-hydroxyvitamin D; then in the kidney, at carbon 1, making the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Parathyroid hormone stimulates that kidney step. F G F 23 and the active hormone itself switch it down.
Vitamin K is the cofactor that carboxylates factors two, seven, nine and ten, and proteins C and S. The used vitamin K is recycled by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, called VKOR.

props.title: A · D · E · K absorbed with fat
Vitamin K cycle
lines: Carboxylates II, VII, IX, X, C, S

scenes.title: When intake is not enough
scenes.altText: Card 1, fat malabsorption: celiac disease, Crohn disease, chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, chronic cholestasis, bowel resection, bariatric surgery; drugs such as orlistat, cholestyramine and mineral-oil laxatives. Result: fat-soluble vitamin deficiency despite adequate intake. Card 2, vitamin K blocked: vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin inhibit VKOR, so vitamin K is depleted and vitamin K-dependent proteins are released undercarboxylated (PIVKA) and inactive. Card 3, newborns: poor placental transfer and little vitamin K in breast milk; vitamin K prophylaxis (intramuscular vitamin K1 1 mg is used worldwide; oral regimens also exist) prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

cues.text: If fat is not absorbed, these vitamins are not absorbed either. Celiac disease, Crohn disease, chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, bowel resection and bariatric surgery can all cause deficiency even when intake is adequate.
Some drugs do the same: orlistat, cholestyramine and mineral-oil laxatives interfere with absorption.
Vitamin K can also be blocked. Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, inhibits VKOR. Vitamin K runs out, and the clotting proteins leave the liver uncarboxylated and inactive, known as PIVKA.

Newborns start low: little vitamin K crosses the placenta and breast milk contains little. That is why vitamin K is given at birth, often as one milligram intramuscularly, to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

props.title: Newborns
lines: Low placental transfer, low in milk

scenes.title: Reading the results
scenes.altText: Card 1, status marker: 25(OH)D — higher concentration and half-life about 3 weeks (vitamin D itself about 1 day); 1,25(OH)₂D is tightly regulated and almost always within normal limits even when 25(OH)D shows deficiency. Card 2, cut-offs (guideline-dependent): <20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) deficiency; <12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) severe; some guidance uses <30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L); ng/mL × 2.496 = nmol/L; hypercalcaemia from intoxication usually only above 375 nmol/L (150 ng/mL). Card 3, when to order 1,25(OH)₂D: granulomatous disease or lymphoma (extrarenal production), CYP27B1 defects, hypophosphataemic disorders. Card 4, vitamin K deficiency: prolonged PT and APTT, raised PIVKA, rapid correction after vitamin K. Hook answers.

cues.text: For vitamin D status, measure 25-hydroxyvitamin D. It circulates at higher concentration and lasts about three weeks. The active hormone is tightly regulated and is almost always within normal limits, even in deficiency.

Common cut-offs: below 20 nanograms per millilitre, or 50 nanomoles per litre, is deficiency, and below 12 is severe. Some guidelines use 30 as the line. Toxic hypercalcaemia usually needs levels above 150 nanograms per millilitre.
Order the active hormone for special questions instead: granulomatous disease, rare enzyme defects, or hypophosphataemic disorders.

Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the P T, the A P T T can lengthen too, PIVKA rises, and clotting times correct quickly after vitamin K. In the hook, the normal active hormone misled; the low 25-hydroxy result and the long P T point to fat malabsorption.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “1,25(OH)₂D tells you vitamin D status” (✓ 25(OH)D does; 1,25(OH)₂D is tightly regulated and usually normal in deficiency); “Adequate intake means adequate fat-soluble vitamin status” (✓ fat malabsorption causes deficiency despite intake); “Vitamin K is needed for factor VIII” (✓ vitamin K-dependent: II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S).

cues.text: Trap one: order the active hormone to check vitamin D status. No: measure 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The active hormone usually stays normal in deficiency.
Trap two: the patient takes supplements, so status must be fine. No: without fat absorption, A, D, E and K are lost.
Trap three: vitamin K deficiency lowers factor eight. No: the vitamin K-dependent proteins are two, seven, nine, ten, and proteins C and S.

props.title: ✗ “Vitamin K makes factor VIII.”
lines: ✓ II, VII, IX, X, C and S

scenes.title: Check the pantry, not the tap
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Check the PANTRY, not the TAP: 25(OH)D is the stock in the pantry; 1,25(OH)₂D is the tap the body keeps running at a steady flow. And vitamin K’s clotting factors spell 1972 — X, IX, VII, II — plus C and S.” Tokens: pantry = 25(OH)D · tap = 1,25(OH)₂D · K = 10, 9, 7, 2 + C, S. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: check the pantry, not the tap. 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the stock in the pantry. The active hormone is a tap the body keeps flowing steadily, so it hides an empty pantry. And vitamin K’s clotting factors spell nineteen seventy-two: ten, nine, seven, two, plus C and S.

Where it breaks: the tap is not always steady. Granulomas can raise the active hormone, and rare enzyme defects lower it, as can some phosphate disorders. Pantry cut-offs differ between guidelines. And the pantry is also filled by sunlight, not just food.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “A, D, E, K need fat absorption · vitamin D status = 25(OH)D, not 1,25(OH)₂D”, “Warfarin blocks VKOR → II, VII, IX, X, C, S uncarboxylated”.

cues.text: Vitamins A, D, E and K need working fat absorption, vitamin D status is judged by 25-hydroxyvitamin D rather than the tightly regulated active hormone, and warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, leaving factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S inactive.

props.label: A, D, E, K need fat absorption · status = 25(OH)D, not 1,25
Warfarin blocks VKOR → II, VII, IX, X, C, S inactive

explanation.what: Plain language: four vitamins (A, D, E, K) travel with fat, so if fat is not absorbed they are lost no matter how many pills are taken. Vitamin D has a stored form you can measure and an active form the body keeps steady, so you measure the stored form. Vitamin K switches on several clotting proteins; warfarin works by stopping vitamin K from being reused. Scientific terms: fat malabsorption, 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)₂D, calcitriol], CYP2R1, CYP27B1, parathyroid hormone (PTH), FGF23, γ-glutamyl carboxylation, vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), vitamin K antagonist (VKA), PIVKA, vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB).
explanation.why: Absorption of fat-soluble vitamins depends on enterocyte, hepatobiliary and pancreatic function, so intestinal, pancreatic and cholestatic disease can cause deficiency. 1,25(OH)₂D is tightly regulated (PTH stimulates the renal 1α-hydroxylation, and poor vitamin D status is linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism), so it is almost always within normal limits while 25(OH)D stores fall. Vitamin K is the cofactor for carboxylation; blocking its recycling by VKOR leaves undercarboxylated, inactive proteins.
explanation.measure: Vitamin D status: serum 25(OH)D (half-life about 3 weeks). Common cut-offs: <20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) deficiency, <12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) severe; some guidance uses <30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L); ng/mL × 2.496 = nmol/L. Intoxication hypercalcaemia usually only above 375 nmol/L (150 ng/mL). 1,25(OH)₂D: for granulomatous disease, CYP27B1 defects and hypophosphataemic disorders. Vitamin K deficiency: prolonged PT (APTT may also be prolonged), raised PIVKA, rapid correction after vitamin K.
explanation.differs: 25(OH)D (stores, status) vs 1,25(OH)₂D (active, tightly regulated); dietary deficiency vs malabsorption (deficiency despite intake); vitamin K-dependent (II, VII, IX, X, C, S) vs not (for example factor VIII).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the vitamin D status test, explain a normal 1,25(OH)₂D in deficiency, link steatorrhoea or pancreatic disease to A, D, E, K deficiency, name the vitamin K-dependent factors, or identify VKOR as the warfarin target.

mnemonic.text: Check the PANTRY, not the TAP: 25(OH)D is the stock in the pantry; 1,25(OH)₂D is the tap the body keeps running steadily. Vitamin K’s clotting factors spell 1972 — X, IX, VII, II — plus C and S.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates the status marker from the regulated hormone and lists the vitamin K-dependent proteins.
mnemonic.limitation: 1,25(OH)₂D can be high (granulomatous disease) or low (CYP27B1 defects; normal to low in FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia); deficiency cut-offs differ by guideline; vitamin D also comes from sunlight, not only diet.

analogyLimitations: Vitamin D cut-offs differ between guidelines and assays.
takeaway: Vitamins A, D, E and K need working fat absorption, vitamin D status is judged by 25-hydroxyvitamin D rather than the tightly regulated active hormone, and warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling, leaving factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S inactive.

questions.stem: A physician wants to know whether a patient has nutritional vitamin D deficiency. Which test is most appropriate?

options.rationale: Correct. 25(OH)D reflects supply from all sources and is the accepted status marker.
Incorrect. It is tightly regulated (PTH stimulates its production) and is almost always normal even in deficiency.
Incorrect. Vitamin D itself has a half-life of only about a day, whereas 25(OH)D (about 3 weeks) is the accepted marker of supply from all sources.
Incorrect. Poor vitamin D status is linked to secondary hyperparathyroidism, but PTH is not a measure of vitamin D status.

questions.stem: A patient with cystic fibrosis and steatorrhoea takes a multivitamin daily but has low vitamin A, vitamin E and 25(OH)D and a prolonged PT. What best explains this?

options.rationale: Correct. Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with fat and need pancreatic enzymes and bile; malabsorption causes deficiency despite intake.

options.text: Excess renal loss of water-soluble vitamins
options.rationale: Incorrect. A, D, E and K are fat-soluble; the pattern points to absorption, not urinary loss.

options.text: The multivitamin contains no fat-soluble vitamins
options.rationale: Incorrect. The key clue is steatorrhoea: even adequate intake is not absorbed without fat digestion.

options.text: Laboratory error, because supplements prevent deficiency
options.rationale: Incorrect. Supplements do not prevent deficiency when fat absorption fails.

questions.stem: How does warfarin produce its anticoagulant effect?

options.text: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so factors II, VII, IX and X are released uncarboxylated
options.rationale: Correct. Blocking VKOR stops vitamin K recycling, leaving the vitamin K-dependent proteins undercarboxylated and inactive.
Incorrect. Direct factor Xa inhibition is the action of drugs such as rivaroxaban and apixaban.

options.text: It blocks synthesis of factor VIII
options.rationale: Incorrect. Factor VIII is not a vitamin K-dependent protein.
Incorrect. Direct thrombin inhibition is the action of drugs such as dabigatran.

claims.text: A, D, E, K absorbed with fat; need enterocyte, hepatobiliary and pancreatic function; malabsorptive diseases, surgery and drugs cause deficiency despite intake.
Liver 25-hydroxylation (CYP2R1) then kidney 1α-hydroxylation (CYP27B1); PTH stimulates, FGF23 and 1,25(OH)₂D inhibit.
25(OH)D is the status marker (half-life about 3 weeks); 1,25(OH)₂D almost always normal in deficiency.
Cut-offs <20 ng/mL deficiency, <12 severe, some use <30; ng/mL × 2.496 = nmol/L; intoxication usually >375 nmol/L.
Indications for 1,25(OH)₂D: granulomatous disease or lymphoma, CYP27B1 defects, hypophosphataemic disorders.
Vitamin K carboxylates II, VII, IX, X, C, S; VKOR recycles it; warfarin/VKAs inhibit VKOR leaving uncarboxylated proteins (PIVKA).

Newborns: poor placental transfer, low breast-milk vitamin K; vitamin K at birth (IM 1 mg used worldwide); deficiency labs: prolonged PT (APTT too in VKDB), raised PIVKA, rapid correction after vitamin K.
Water-soluble vitamin deficiency within weeks; B12 stores 3–6 years; PT rises only when undercarboxylated prothrombin passes 50%; 1,25(OH)₂D “even high” in deficiency; toxicity >500 nmol/L.
claims.note: Reviewer statements not verified against an open source read in this session; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 27 Hit 6 and the Number Vault give a vitamin D “target ~30 ng/mL”. Sources read differ by body: Amrein 2020 names >20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) as the primary treatment goal and notes that most authors consider <30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) deficiency; Pilz 2019 reports the Endocrine Society guideline recommends treating to at least 75 nmol/L, while the IOM report does not conclude there is added benefit of 75 over 50 nmol/L (register flag rv-vitd-target-guideline). Philippine guidance was not reviewed.

Ch. 27 Hit 6 gives vitamin D toxicity as >500 nmol/L (Number Vault ~200 ng/mL). Pilz 2019 and Amrein 2020 report intoxication hypercalcaemia usually above 375 nmol/L (150 ng/mL), and the IOM classes sustained >125 nmol/L as potentially harmful; the lesson teaches the source figures (register flag rv-vitd-toxicity-threshold).
